en: The *Sūtra on Yaṅkī* Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Song dynasty layman Juqu Jingsheng.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was in the kingdom of Kānyākubja. In that kingdom, there was a great brahmin...
There was a man of wealthy lineage named Yajñika who had previously practiced ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths in his quest for blessings and protection.

He heard that by serving the Buddha, one attains wealth, nobility, long life, and peace; one is delivered from birth and death to receive blessings, does not enter the three evil realms, and no longer undergoes arduous suffering.
Yajña thought to himself,
"It would be better for me to set aside these non-Buddhists and instead serve the Buddha.
He then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head to the ground in salutation, knelt on both knees, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I was originally ignorant and lacked all understanding; yet I have heard in secret that the Buddha-way is vast and expansive, with great compassion that universally rescues all. The Buddha is the most honored among gods, humans, and those above and below heaven; there is none who does not find peace and stability."
"I now wish to set aside the non-Buddhist practices I have followed and take refuge in the Buddha. May the Buddha have compassion for me and please accept my request for instruction.
The Buddha said, "What you have just said is most excellent!"
"If one reflects deeply upon this and ceases evil to practice goodness, why should one worry about not attaining peace and security?
Yajñika said to the Buddha,
"Since that which I previously served was not true, I now take refuge in the Buddha."
"Please have compassion for us, abandon these defiled and impure practices, and accept the Buddha’s pure and definitive word.
If this is indeed so, it would be most excellent.
Yajñadatta then stepped forward and received the five precepts.
First, abstaining from taking life;
second, abstaining from stealing;
third, abstaining from sexual misconduct.
Fourth, one must refrain from double-tongued speech, harsh words, lying, and frivolous chatter;
fifth, one must not drink alcohol.
Having performed the threefold refuge, he rose and circumambulated the Buddha three times, observed the fast for seven days, and then departed.
From that time forward, when he traveled to other countries, he would desire to follow those who killed living beings for sport, hunted, or stole others' property;
he would feel covetousness upon seeing women of beautiful appearance;
and whenever he saw people doing right or wrong, he would immediately comment on it.
Seeing someone drinking wine and becoming intoxicated and disorderly, he wished to pursue them; his mind was unsettled and he further desired to repent. He thought to himself:
"I am unable to practice this Buddha-dharma; in the end, I shall return the five precepts to the Buddha."
He immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and said:

"Previously, I received the five precepts from the Buddha; however, there are many prohibitions and restrictions that prevent me from following my own inclinations. Now, reflecting upon this myself, I wish to desist and am unable to continue serving the Buddha."
"The Buddha-Dharma is revered; it is not something I am capable of serving. May I then receive back the five precepts?
Would this be acceptable to the Buddha's mind?
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond. Before his words had even left his mouth, a natural spirit appeared, wielding an iron mallet to strike Yajñika on the head and shatter it.
Furthermore, there are spirits and ghosts who strip away their garments;
others who, using iron hooks, pull out their tongues from their mouths;
and there are harlot spirits who deeply cut off their sexual organs with knives.
There were spirits and ghosts who poured molten copper into his mouth;
before, behind, to the left, and to the right, various spirits and ghosts vied with one another to tear apart his flesh.

Thus, Yajñadatta’s eyes were filled with stinking tears, and his face turned the color of earth; natural fires burned his body, such that he could not seek life nor could he seek death, as the spirits and ghosts held him with extreme urgency.
The Buddha, seeing him in this state, felt compassion for him and asked Yajñeya, "What do you intend to do now?
Yajñeya’s mouth was so parched he could no longer speak; he could only raise his hand to strike himself, seeking mercy from the Buddha.
The Buddha then manifested his majestic spiritual power, and the ghosts and spirits were all terrified and fled.
Yaṣka was able to recover his breath; rising again, he prostrated himself with his head at [the Buddha's] feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Within my heart there are these five thieves who drag me into evil transgressions and cause me to utter such wicked words."
"Now I am receiving this retribution because I myself acted in violation of the Buddha’s words; I pray that the Buddha will have compassion for me.
The Buddha said, "As for what was done by your own mind and mouth, whom else should you blame?"
Yaṣka addressed the Buddha, saying:

"From this day forward, I shall reform myself and uphold the five precepts; I shall observe the three fast days of the year and the six fast days of the month, burning incense and lighting lamps to serve the Triple Gem, and I dare not again transgress in body, speech, or mind."
The Buddha said, "So it is;

excellent! Whatever is seen by the eyes and whatever is experienced by the body, one receives the fruits of one's own actions. By doing good, one obtains good; by conceiving unwholesome thoughts, one obtains what is unwholesome."

The Buddha is the teacher among all dharmas; he teaches people to abandon evil and practice good, so that they may ultimately attain liberation. He causes all devas and humans, as well as those who are ignorant and deluded, to possess wisdom and no longer undergo toil and suffering.
"From this day forward, you shall reform and cultivate goodness; do not allow yourself to follow the dictates of your mind and heart, which lead people astray at their very root.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Yajñika’s mind was opened and liberated; he immediately attained the stage of Srotāpanna and departed with joy.

When Yaṣka returned home, he immediately commanded all members of his household, both great and small, to go to the Buddha’s presence and receive the five precepts, observing the three seasonal fasts and the six monthly fasts.
Yaṣka then renounced his home, shaved his hair and beard, donned the *kāṣāya*, followed the Buddha as a *śramaṇa*, and eventually attained the path of an Arhat.
The Sūtra on Yaśas Spoken by the Buddha
